description:
**Team BÖVD** 🌌
> Our name comes from the Boötes Void, one of the largest empty regions in the universe. Astronauts face their own kind of void: far from home, with no doctor in the room. We're building BÖVD, an AI health monitor for astronauts that reads live data from NASA's ISS feed (cabin oxygen, CO₂, pressure and temperature) and shows how the station's environment affects the crew's vitals.
summary: BÖVD is an offline health-monitoring app that lets astronauts check their own health on the ISS, on the Moon, in Mars transit and on Mars. An astronaut enters a measurement such as heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature, sleep or mood. The app compares it first with that astronaut's own baseline, adjusted for the current gravity, and then with NASA and clinical reference ranges and recent trends. It then gives four clear answers: the status (green, yellow or red), why, the next step to take, and who to contact. Alerts go from the crew to the Crew Medical Officer and on to the flight surgeon over a simulated Earth link with the real Moon or Mars delay, so the crew is never left waiting for an answer from Earth. Every reading and threshold shows its source, and the app loads real NASA data from the Open Science Data Repository (study OSD-575, SpaceX Inspiration4). This matters because on a Mars mission a message to Earth takes 4–24 minutes one way. The crew must be able to understand and act on their own health data, and BÖVD gives them clear, explained guidance without needing medical training.
details:
What it does

  • Records health indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, temperature, blood glucose, sleep, mood, stress, workload, cabin CO₂, radiation dose, body mass, exercise and urine values. Input is by keyboard, file import (CSV, FHIR) or camera (posture check only).
  • Rates each value green, yellow or red and adds them into one 0–20 status score, shown on a ring and a clickable 3D human body.
  • Explains every result in a "Why" panel: which spaceflight hazard it relates to, what rule fired, the next steps, who to contact and the scientific sources.
  • Sends alerts at three priority levels from the crew to the Crew Medical Officer and to the ground flight surgeon, with a store-and-forward queue that simulates the Moon (≈1.3 s) and Mars (4–24 min) communication delay.
  • Covers all five NASA hazards of human spaceflight: radiation (personal dose map and solar-storm shelter mode), isolation (sleep, mood and crew-harmony trends), distance (7 offline "Smart Doctor" protocols), gravity (gravity-aware baselines and a post-landing stand test) and closed environment (cabin CO₂ judged at the actual cabin pressure).
  • Five roles with different access: astronaut, Crew Medical Officer, behavioral health specialist, flight surgeon and researcher.
  • Gives guidance for all 17 indicators: why each check matters in space and how to stay healthy and prevent a critical condition, with sources.
  • Optional NASA-grounded AI research assistant on the Smart Doctor page: a free OpenRouter model answers the astronaut's questions only from 116 bundled NASA and CSA excerpts and cites each one. It never diagnoses, and only the typed question leaves the device, with consent.
  • Full 16-slide presentation: https://github.com/al8a7aa/bovd5/blob/main/BOVD/deliverables/English/BOVD_Full_Presentation.pdf

How it works Validation → personal baseline (mean ± 2 SD of the astronaut's own early-flight or pre-flight readings) → reference thresholds → trend rules (for example, 3 short nights in a row turns red) → composite score → explanation and alert. All thresholds are in configuration files with a citation for each one, so a flight surgeon can review and change them. The app never diagnoses; it gives status, explanation, next step and who to contact.

Benefits

  • Works with no internet or Earth link, which suits Moon and Mars missions.
  • Easy to understand for non-doctors: colours with icons and labels, plain-language explanations, a guided tour, large-button "glove mode", high contrast, Arabic and English.
  • Every value shows where it came from (REAL, SYNTHETIC or USER-ENTERED) and every rule shows its source.
  • Health data stays on the device and is encrypted (AES-256-GCM); each feature asks for consent first.

What we hope to achieve A tool that crews on the Artemis Moon base and future Mars missions could use for Earth-independent medical care. The same approach also fits Antarctic stations and remote clinics on Earth. Next steps: a flight-surgeon review of every threshold, more NASA data, a neutron-dose input similar to the CSA's CANS instrument, and usability tests with gloves in an analog mission.

Tools and languages Python 3 (standard library only) for the server and the assessment engine; SQLite for storage; HTML, CSS and JavaScript with WebGL for the interface and the 3D body; FHIR R4 with LOINC codes for health records. Optional: OpenCV and MediaPipe for the camera posture check, and the cryptography library for faster encryption. Optional AI assistant through the OpenRouter API (free model router openrouter/free). Tested with pytest (151 automated tests). Starts on Windows by double-clicking start.bat; on macOS and Linux with ./start.sh, or with Docker.
